facts: Loudcloud's IPO roadshow opened at $10 a share; with comparable companies losing about half their value during the roadshow, it was repriced to $6, and the IPO raised $162.5 million.
The company's filing said it would run out of money in about three weeks without the IPO.
After its first earnings call, revenue guidance was cut from $75 million to $55 million and the stock fell from $6 to $2.
Loudcloud's customers, many of them internet companies, were going bankrupt; its largest customer, paying about $1 million a month (about 20% of revenue), went bankrupt in early 2002.
Horowitz considered bankruptcy, then decided to build the company around the Opsware server-management software and exit the cloud business.
Loudcloud sold the cloud business to EDS for $63.5 million in cash; EDS also licensed Opsware for $20 million a year. IBM was the other leading bidder.
The company kept the Opsware product and renamed itself Opsware.
Horowitz's point in the book: no management book gave a formula for these moments.

Loudcloud was founded in 1999 by Horowitz and Marc Andreessen; two months later it raised $21 million, and investors urged Horowitz to run it as if capital were free. Within six months it hired almost 200 people and spent $5 million on an office.
In June 2000 it closed a $120 million round at a $700 million pre-money valuation; late in 2000 it had 477 employees; Q3 2000 bookings were $37 million against a $100 million forecast.
Its filing showed $1.94 million in revenue over the prior six months and forecast $75 million for the coming year.
Competitor Exodus went bankrupt on 26 September 2001, a year after being valued at $50 billion.
Horowitz put a team of ten on making Opsware run on any server platform and kept the plan from the rest of the company so it would not distract from the core business.
In 2007 HP bought Opsware for about $1.6 billion.
scene_details: a roadshow price cut from $10 to $6
a filing that names three weeks of cash
a customer paying $1 million a month going bankrupt
the sale of the business the company had been built on
tension: The company had to sell the business it was built on to keep the product it hardly sold.
opening_idea: Open on the roadshow price cut from $10 to $6.

lessons.idea: When every option is bad, picking the least-bad one in the open and early beats waiting for a clean answer.
lessons.anchor: selling the cloud business to EDS and keeping Opsware

reflect_final: Which decision are you postponing because every option looks bad, and what is the least-bad choice you could name aloud this week?

use_cases.situation: Your team keeps debating two bad options.
use_cases.move: Name the less-bad one aloud with the reason and a date, as Horowitz did when he chose to sell the core business to keep the product.

use_cases.situation: You must tell someone bad news about their role.
use_cases.move: Say the facts first, plainly, without softening the decision itself.

use_cases.situation: You are stuck choosing between two costly paths in your own life.
use_cases.move: Write what each option costs and pick the cost you can live with.

pocket_idea: Horowitz sold the business he had built to keep the product; a clean answer was never coming.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Loudcloud had three weeks of cash on paper and a price cut from $10 to $6 before it even listed.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Loudcloud went public in 2001 after repricing from $10 to $6, with a filing that warned of three weeks of cash. The stock fell, customers went bankrupt, and Horowitz sold the cloud business to EDS for $63.5 million to keep the Opsware software, which EDS then licensed.
conversation_variants.question_idea: What decision are you putting off because no option is good?
